prompt: An online retailer's website traffic rose 30% this year, but orders were flat.
flawed_answer: Traffic has likely grown faster than orders this year.
right_parts: it is framed as likely, not as settled fact
model_repair: The new visitors are probably less ready to buy than past ones, so fewer visits end in an order. I'd compare conversion by traffic source this year and last.

prompt: A call center's cost per call rose 20%, while wages stayed the same.
flawed_answer: A new phone system is slowing agents, so it has to be replaced.
right_parts: it names a specific cause rather than a vague one
model_repair: Calls are probably taking longer, maybe because the new phone system slows agents. I'd check average handle time by month and call type before replacing anything.

prompt: A restaurant's food waste doubled in three months. Its menu grew from 20 to 35 dishes over the same period.
flawed_answer: Ordering, storage, portions and staff habits are probably involved.
right_parts: it is framed as likely ("probably"), not as settled fact
model_repair: With 35 dishes instead of 20, more ingredients are probably expiring before they're used. I'd compare waste by ingredient with how many dishes use each one.

prompt: A hospital's supply costs rose 18% in two years. Patient volumes and the number of items used per patient were both flat.
flawed_answer: Supply spending has probably drifted out of control.
right_parts: it is framed as likely ("probably") and is about supply costs
model_repair: With volumes and items per patient flat, the hospital is probably paying more per item, perhaps by buying off-contract. I'd compare unit prices paid for the top supplies with contract prices.

prompt: A delivery company's on-time rate fell from 96% to 88% in six months. Order volume rose 25% over the same period.
flawed_answer: Traffic, weather, routing and staffing each probably contribute something.
right_parts: it is framed as likely ("probably"), not as settled fact
model_repair: Capacity has probably lagged the 25% rise in orders, so drivers can't finish their routes on time. I'd compare on-time rates with stops per driver by route.

prompt: A bank opened 10 branches in a new city. Accounts opened per branch are 40% below plan, while foot traffic is on plan.
flawed_answer: Branch staff are poorly trained, and retraining will fix it.
right_parts: it looks for why visitors who come in don't open accounts
model_repair: Branch staff are probably not turning visitors into accounts, perhaps from weak training. I'd compare accounts opened per visitor by branch and by how long staff have worked there.

prompt: A city's bus ridership fell 15% in two years while the population grew 3%. Average trip times rose 20%.
flawed_answer: People have probably soured on the buses.
right_parts: it is framed as likely ("probably")
model_repair: Trips are 20% slower, so riders are probably switching to driving. I'd compare ridership changes on the routes that slowed most against those that slowed least.

prompt: A hospital's revenue per patient fell 9% while patient numbers held steady. The share of patients on government insurance rose from 30% to 45%.
flawed_answer: Payer mix, coding, services and billing probably contribute.
right_parts: it is framed as likely ("probably"), not as settled fact
model_repair: The rise from 30% to 45% of patients on government insurance, which pays less, is probably cutting revenue per patient. I'd compare revenue per patient by payer across the two years.

prompt: After a 10% fare increase, a ferry operator's revenue per passenger rose 10% this year, but its total ticket revenue was flat.
flawed_answer: Something about demand has probably shifted.
right_parts: it is framed as likely ("probably")
model_repair: The higher fares probably drove some passengers away: flat revenue with 10% more per passenger means about 9% fewer passengers. I'd compare passenger changes by route with each route's fare rise.

prompt: A subscription box company's revenue grew 20% this year while its customer count grew 50%. The price of a box was unchanged.
flawed_answer: New-customer discounts have clearly cut the price per box.
right_parts: it looks for why revenue grew more slowly than customers
model_repair: Revenue per customer fell about 20% with the box price unchanged, so customers are probably taking fewer boxes, perhaps skipping months. I'd compare boxes per customer by joining date and plan.

prompt: A sandwich chain's revenue is flat, but its profit fell 20%. Food costs rose from 30% to 32% of revenue.
flawed_answer: Something on the cost side has probably gone wrong.
right_parts: it is framed as likely ("probably") and points to costs
model_repair: Ingredient prices have probably risen faster than menu prices, pushing food from 30% to 32% of revenue. I'd compare ingredient costs per sandwich with menu prices over the year.

prompt: A US snack brand launched in the UK a year ago. Trial was strong: 20% of shoppers bought it once. But only a quarter of those buyers bought it again.
flawed_answer: UK shoppers clearly dislike the flavors, so the brand has to pull out.
right_parts: it ties the problem to the product after people try it, which fits weak repeat buying
model_repair: The product probably disappoints UK shoppers once they try it, perhaps the flavors, since only a quarter rebuy. I'd survey one-time buyers and compare repeat rates by flavor.

prompt: A coffee chain's morning sales are up 5%, but afternoon sales are down 20%. Two months ago, a bubble-tea chain opened next to most of its stores.
flawed_answer: Afternoon sales have likely fallen while morning sales held up.
right_parts: it is framed as likely, not as settled fact
model_repair: Afternoon buyers are probably trying the new bubble-tea shops next door, since only afternoons fell. I'd compare afternoon sales at stores with and without a bubble-tea shop nearby.

prompt: A car wash's revenue fell 15% last year. The number of cars washed was flat.
flawed_answer: Revenue has likely fallen while the number of cars stayed steady, so revenue per car is down.
right_parts: it is framed as likely, not as settled fact
model_repair: Customers are probably choosing the basic wash over premium, so revenue per car fell 15%. I'd compare the mix of wash types sold this year and last.

prompt: A trucking company's fuel cost per mile rose 12%, while diesel prices rose 4%. Its fleet's average age went from 4 to 7 years.
flawed_answer: Fuel cost per mile has likely risen faster than diesel prices, by about 8 points.
right_parts: it is framed as likely and uses the gap between the 12% and the 4%
model_repair: Older trucks are probably burning more fuel per mile: fuel cost per mile rose 12% while diesel rose only 4%, as the fleet aged from 4 to 7 years. I'd compare miles per gallon by truck age.

prompt: A yogurt brand launched a plant-based line. Sales reached 50% of target, and 70% of buyers were already buyers of the brand's dairy yogurt.
flawed_answer: The new line is eating into dairy sales, so it should be dropped at once.
right_parts: it uses the fact that most buyers already buy the brand's dairy yogurt
model_repair: The line probably isn't reaching shoppers beyond our base, since 70% of buyers already buy our dairy yogurt. I'd compare how many new households bought it against plan.

prompt: An e-commerce warehouse's error rate on orders tripled after it hired 40 seasonal workers.
flawed_answer: New staff, training, labels and layout are probably each part of it.
right_parts: it is framed as likely ("probably") and includes the new staff
model_repair: The 40 new seasonal workers are probably making most of the extra picking errors. I'd compare error rates by worker, new against experienced.

prompt: A craft brewery's sales in bars fell 10%, while its supermarket sales rose 25%.
flawed_answer: Bar sales have likely fallen while supermarket sales grew.
right_parts: it is framed as likely, not as settled fact
model_repair: Drinkers are probably moving from bars to drinking at home, shifting our sales to supermarkets. I'd compare industry-wide bar and supermarket beer sales with ours over the year.

prompt: A regional airline has lost money for three years. Its planes fly 70% full, while the industry average is 82%.
flawed_answer: Planes are probably full, leaving no room for more passengers. I'd compare seats sold with seats flown by route.
right_parts: it is framed as likely and names data to check: seats sold against seats flown by route
model_repair: Planes are probably flying too empty to cover costs, 70% full against an 82% industry average. I'd compare seats sold with seats flown by route.

prompt: A state's unemployment office processes claims in 21 days on average, against a 10-day target. Claims volume is flat, but staff fell 30%.
flawed_answer: A surge in claims has likely swamped the office. I'd check claims handled per staff member each week.
right_parts: it is framed as likely and names data to check: claims handled per staff member each week
model_repair: Losing 30% of staff has probably left too few people to handle a flat claims volume. I'd check claims handled per staff member each week, before and after the cuts.

prompt: A gym chain's membership grew 10% last year, but revenue grew only 2%.
flawed_answer: Discounts, cheaper plans, training sales and billing errors likely all play a part.
right_parts: it is framed as likely, not as settled fact
model_repair: Growth probably came from discounted plans, cutting revenue per member. I'd compare revenue per member by plan type and joining date, this year against last.

prompt: A software company's revenue grew 25%, but its operating margin fell from 20% to 8%. Headcount grew 60%.
flawed_answer: Cloud hosting costs have probably jumped with the extra revenue. I'd compare hosting costs with revenue by quarter.
right_parts: it is framed as likely and compares a cost with revenue by quarter
model_repair: Hiring has probably run ahead of revenue: headcount grew 60% against 25% revenue growth. I'd compare payroll with revenue by quarter.

prompt: A pizza chain's same-store sales fell 8% this year. A new competitor opened in 40% of its markets.
flawed_answer: The competitor caused the decline, so prices need to be cut to match.
right_parts: it names the new competitor as the cause
model_repair: The new competitor is probably taking share in the markets it entered. I'd compare same-store sales in those 40% of markets with the rest.

prompt: A factory's output per shift fell 12% after it installed new packing machines. Machine downtime is reported as normal.
flawed_answer: The new machines are probably breaking down more than the old ones. I'd compare output by shift and by machine.
right_parts: it is framed as likely and names output data to check: output by shift and by machine
model_repair: Workers are probably still learning the new machines, since downtime is normal. I'd compare output per shift by machine and by how long each crew has used it.

prompt: A beverage company's new energy drink sells well in convenience stores but poorly in supermarkets, where it has half the shelf space of rivals.
flawed_answer: Shelf space, price, promotions and shopper type are probably all part of it.
right_parts: it is framed as likely ("probably") and includes shelf space
model_repair: Having half the shelf space of rivals is probably holding back supermarket sales. I'd compare sales per store in supermarkets that give it more space with those that don't.

prompt: A company bought a competitor two years ago, expecting $20M a year in cost savings. Savings so far are $8M a year, and the two IT systems still run separately.
flawed_answer: The $20M target was likely unrealistic from the start. I'd compare it with savings in similar deals.
right_parts: it is framed as likely and names a comparison to check
model_repair: The separate IT systems are probably blocking the savings that need shared processes. I'd compare savings achieved with plan, split by whether each saving needs merged IT.

prompt: A grocery chain opened five stores in a new state. Traffic is on plan, but the average basket is 30% smaller than in its home state.
flawed_answer: The new stores are likely drawing less traffic than planned. I'd compare visits per store with the plan by week.
right_parts: it is framed as likely, not as settled fact
model_repair: My hypothesis is that shoppers use the new stores for top-up trips rather than a weekly shop, so baskets are 30% smaller. I'd compare items per basket with the home state's by week.

prompt: A children's clothing brand sells 70% of its products online. Online growth slowed from 30% to 5% a year, and new online customers fell by half, though ad spend was unchanged. Store sales grew 10%.
flawed_answer: Online probably isn't working the way it used to.
right_parts: it is framed as likely ("probably") and points to online
model_repair: The brand has probably reached most of the new parents its ads can find online, since new customers halved at the same ad spend. I'd compare ad reach and cost per new customer by month.

prompt: A ride-hailing company's share in one city fell from 60% to 45% in six months after a rival cut prices 20%. The company's own prices were unchanged.
flawed_answer: Price is the only factor, so the company needs to match the cut now.
right_parts: it ties the loss of share to the rival's price cut
model_repair: Price-sensitive riders are probably switching to the cheaper rival. I'd compare which riders left, by trip type and how often they rode, with riders who stayed.

prompt: A university's energy costs rose 25% in a year, while energy prices rose 10%. It opened two new buildings.
flawed_answer: The new buildings are inefficient and need to be retrofitted.
right_parts: it ties the extra cost to the two new buildings
model_repair: The two new buildings probably use much of the extra energy, since prices explain only 10% of the 25% rise. I'd meter the new buildings' use against the rest of campus.

prompt: An airline cut fares 10% on one route, where most passengers are business travelers. Passengers rose 6%, and revenue on the route fell.
flawed_answer: The fare cut probably didn't land the way it was meant to.
right_parts: it is framed as likely ("probably") and is about the fare cut
model_repair: Business travelers probably fly whatever the fare, so the 10% cut gave revenue away for only 6% more passengers. I'd compare passengers by traveler type before and after the cut.

prompt: A meal-kit company acquires customers at $90 each. Half cancel within two months, and the average customer orders four boxes with $25 margin each.
flawed_answer: Customers likely bring about $100 of margin against $90 to acquire, so each one barely pays back.
right_parts: it is framed as likely, and its math is right: four boxes at $25 is about $100 against $90
model_repair: The half who cancel within two months probably never pay back their $90, while those who stay lift the average to about $100. I'd compare margin per customer by how long they stayed.

prompt: A hotel renovated half its rooms. Renovated rooms sell for 25% more per night and are 70% full, against 80% full for the old rooms.
flawed_answer: Price, booking channels, room features and guest mix may all be at work.
right_parts: it includes price as a factor
model_repair: The 25% higher rate probably more than makes up for lower occupancy: 1.25 × 70% beats 80%. I'd compare revenue per available room for renovated and old rooms by month.

prompt: A dental practice's patient visits grew 8%, but profit fell 10%. It hired two hygienists last year.
flawed_answer: The practice overhired and needs to let one hygienist go.
right_parts: it ties the profit drop to the two hygienists hired
model_repair: The two new hygienists probably added cost faster than they added visits. I'd compare each hygienist's booked hours and revenue with their pay.

prompt: A software company moved from a one-time license of $1,200 to a $40-a-month subscription. New customers rose 50%, but first-year revenue per customer fell 60%.
flawed_answer: Customers clearly see the subscription as worse value and are leaving, so the company has to return to licenses.
right_parts: it looks at whether customers renew the subscription
model_repair: More customers probably signed up at the lower entry price, and each pays off if they stay past 30 months ($1,200 ÷ $40). I'd track whether customers renew, by monthly sign-up group.

prompt: A manufacturer's new plant runs at 55% of capacity a year after opening, with no unusual downtime. The demand forecast had assumed 85%.
flawed_answer: Machine breakdowns are clearly limiting output, so the plant needs new equipment.
right_parts: it looks for why the plant runs below the 85% planned
model_repair: Demand probably fell short of the forecast, since the plant runs at 55% with normal downtime. I'd compare orders received with the forecast by product and customer.

prompt: A bookstore's sales of books rose 4%, but its total sales fell 6%. Last year, gifts and toys made up 30% of sales.
flawed_answer: Gift and toy sales likely dipped slightly, about 6%. I'd compare gift and toy sales by month with last year.
right_parts: it is framed as likely, looks at gifts and toys, and names data to check: gift and toy sales by month
model_repair: Gift and toy sales have probably fallen about 30%: with books, 70% of sales, up 4%, nothing smaller explains a 6% total fall. I'd compare gift and toy sales by month with last year.

prompt: A client estimates the city's coffee shop market at $40M from industry data. Its three stores make $3M a year, and it believes it has 25% share because it owns 3 of the city's 12 coffee shops.
flawed_answer: Market size, share, store count and missing rivals may all be off here.
right_parts: it questions the share estimate
model_repair: The 25% probably counts shops rather than sales; by sales, $3M of $40M is 7.5%. I'd compare sales per shop for the client and its rivals.

prompt: A clinic's patient visits rose 15%, doctors' hours were unchanged, average visit length was unchanged, and average wait time doubled.
flawed_answer: Patients are probably less patient than they used to be.
right_parts: it is framed as likely ("probably"), not as settled fact
model_repair: The clinic was probably near full capacity, so 15% more visits with the same doctor hours sharply lengthened queues. I'd compare wait times with visits per doctor-hour by day.

prompt: A home-goods retailer's gross margin rose from 30% to 33%, but the margin on each product was unchanged.
flawed_answer: The retailer has probably raised prices across the board. I'd compare sales by category this year and last.
right_parts: it is framed as likely and names data to check: sales by category, this year against last
model_repair: Sales have probably shifted toward higher-margin products, since each product's margin is unchanged. I'd compare each category's share of sales and its margin, this year against last.
